perceived_rprob[trial_i] <- normal(rightprob[trial_i], rightprob[trial_i]*prob_m+prob_offset);

perceived_rprob[trial_i] ~ normal(rightprob[trial_i], rightprob[trial_i]*prob_m+prob_offset);

    int nTrials;

Sorry - it was a silly mistake on my part. The issue is the following: if you use an assignment operator '<-', you need to use normal_rng(). Are you trying to generate fake data, then sample from it? If so, then you want to generate fake data using normal_rng because you want Stan to generate (pseudo)-random samples from a normal. 

If this is the case, may I suggest the following: you generate the data in one Stan file, using the 'generated quantities' block as below (obviously you need to pass it data, etc.) To do this use the algorithm='Fixed_param' option when you call stan in R; you won't have any parameters in your model so you need to tell Stan not to look for them.

generated quantities{
 real perceived_rprob[nTrials];
  ....

  for(trial_i in 1:nTrials){
       perceived_rprob[trial_i] <- normal_rng(rightprob[trial_i], rightprob[trial_i]*prob_m+prob_offset);
        ...   
   }

}


You then collect the samples for your various objects, and then fit your model using (in a separate Stan file):

model{
    for (trial_i in 1:NTrials){
        ....
        choices_01[trial_i] ~ bernoulli_logit(lambda*(Rval-Lval));
    }

}


There may be a way to fit it all in one Stan file, but think doing the above makes life easier.

Let me know if the above is what you want, and makes sense.

parts:
Christine,

I believe this would be simplified if you think more generatively.  The idea is to
build your model to mimic the data generating process itself.  For example, in
a simple Binomial experiment we have some latent “true” probability of success
that we measure in a finite number of trials,

k ~ Binomial(N, p);

and we infer p from k and N.  This can be made much more complicated, with
different p for many different individuals or trials, or having p be a function of 
covariates (leading to logistic regression), etc.

I don’t fully understand the model that you are trying to build, but it sounds like
there are some data censoring issues.  For example, having just (k / N) instead
of k and N separately makes this drastically more complicated because you
can’t exactly recover the likelihood.  

Having some empirical p = k / N, call it p_hat, along with some estimate of the 
standard deviation also runs into problems because the Gaussian approximation 
is valid only for true p away from the 0 and 1 boundaries.  To avoid issues we
recommend treating such convolutions on the logit scale, for example

logit_obs_prop ~ normal(logit_latent_prob, m * log_latent_prob + offset).

That said, I would be very hesitant in this particular model as it is very hard to
derive from any reasonable generative model (I understand the psycophysical
literature might support it, but statistical misunderstandings are rampant in
many, many fields).  

So long story short, the kind of model you want (latent parameters that aren’t
directly observed with hierarchical structure) is very much appropriate for Stan
but at the moment you’re likely being limited by some of the assumptions in
your model.

It would help if you could simplify your model to just the essence of what
you’re trying to fit and then it would be much easier for us to comment and
make more explicit recommendations.

Then when you have the "~" statement it tries to compute the log density at the value on the left of the "~", which isn't going to work if it doesn't yet have a value. You'll either need to declare that variable as an unknown parameter in the parameters block, or keep it in the model block but give it a value. If it's something you're trying to estimate then the former and if it's observed (or a function of observed variables) then the latter.

I was referring to dropping left and right and just having one set of latent
probabilities, although, upon a more careful look, that would be tricky with
the final likelihood depending on both.

While I don’t full grok your model, there are definitely some issues.  In
particular, you definitely don’t want to do this:
perceived_rprob[trial_i] <- normal(rightprob[trial_i], rightprob[trial_i]*prob_m+prob_offset);

which assigns perceived_rprob[trial_i] the value of the normal density and
doesn’t make any statistical sense.

If I understand this correctly, then the model that you want to build is that each user 
in each trial makes a choice based on the difference between Lval and Rval, 
which themselves are based on the user’s perceived left and right probabilities.  
Those perceptions are assumed to be based on the true left and right probabilities, 
which are assumed to be known exactly by the model.

In this case the first big change that you need is to make the perceived
probabilities (and volumes) latent variables, in other words they should all
be parameters sampled by the model.  In the end you marginalize out over
all of these latent perceptions to get at the parameters you care about
while incorporating the uncertainty in not knowing the users’ perceptions
exactly.

Another big modeling issue (the one I had previously referenced) is that the
normal really isn’t compatible with probabilities.  So something like
perceived_rprob[trial_i] ~ normal(rightprob[trial_i], rightprob[trial_i]*prob_m+prob_offset)

will lead to an awkward posterior.  What you want for perceived_rprob[trial_i] is a
distribution over probabilities, such as a beta distribution.  We don’t have a mean/variance
parameterization of the beta so you’d have to do this yourself, but it would conceptually
be similar to the above only more appropriate for probabilities.  

Alternatively you could unconstrained everything and then use the normal without
issue, for example

logit_perceived_rprob[trial_i] <- normal(logit_rightprob[trial_i], exp(logit_rightprob[trial_i] * prob_m + prob_offset))

but then you run into problems where some of the rightprob[trial_i] are exactly 0 and 1.

I know you said that the perception variances are supposed to vary in this way and
I am in no way claiming that I am experienced in your field, but these kinds of
conceptual conflicts are _huge_ red flags that almost always indicate that there’s
tension between claims and the underlying statistics.

Finally, the calculation of Lval and Rval introduces some numerical awkwardness that
is going to induce posteriors that are hard to fit.  There are hints of the Folk Theorem
again, now here suggesting another form, but I’ll just leave a warning here and we
can consider it later.

Yes!  The problem is that you can’t quantify the uncertainty about parameters that you care about
without first quantifying the uncertainty in those unobserved perceptions.  In other words, in order
for the model to learn the interesting parameters it must first learn the perceptions.  

A cool side effect of this is that you can start analyzing those learned perceptions to potentially
say some interesting things about the experiential population.

I know you said that the perception variances are supposed to vary in this way and I am in no way claiming that I am experienced in your field, but these kinds of conceptual conflicts are _huge_ red flags that almost always indicate that there’s tension between claims and the underlying statistics.

Just to clarify, perception variances have been reported to vary in this way for potentially unbounded stimuli (e.g., estimation of stimulus intensity, time, magnitudes, etc.)  These variances are not thought to apply to perception of probability.  What is unique to my experiment is that I am using stimuli that cause this particular perception variance to convey probability to the subject.  Anyway, not sure if that is helpful/useful at all, but it's a weird artifact of my experiment (I have my reasons, but we'll leave it there).

You just have to get those reasons to align with the statistics!  ;-)

In a very real sense the logit probabilities are equivalent to unbounded stimuli
and hence it would be appropriate to model the logit perception probabilities
that way.  This is one of the big motivations of general linear models.
I think the first thing I will try is to unconstrain everything, as you suggest.  On trials where p=1, I suppose I can set it to p=.999?

This is the open question to which I do not have a great answer.  Setting
those extremes to 0.999 might work okay but I couldn’t guarantee it.  You
might have to resort to a probabilistic model, for example with beta distributions.
